title: Like a trumpeter
hookLine: a mind of kindness fills the first direction, then the second, third and fourth, above and below (DN 13)

cards: At dawn, someone stands at the edge of a village with a conch shell, takes one deep breath, and blows. The sound doesn't pick who hears it. It rolls out east, west, north and south.

The farmer hears it, the child hears it, and so does the neighbor who doesn't like the conch blower. Reaching one more house takes no extra effort. An old Buddhist text uses that picture for what a kind mind can do.

teach.b: The text is the Tevijja Sutta, from ten days ago: two young brahmins, Vasettha and Bharadvaja, asking the Buddha the way to union with Brahma. He answers in their own terms.
He describes a monk who lets his mind, full of kindness, pervade one direction, then the second, the third, the fourth.
Then above, below, across, everywhere, the whole wide world, with a mind abundant, grown great, measureless, free of hatred and ill will.

teach.h: A HORN HEARD EVERYWHERE, WITHOUT STRAIN.
teach.b: Then the image: like a strong conch blower who makes himself heard in all four directions without strain.
In the same way, the text says, nothing is left out or passed over. And the same sweep is repeated for compassion, for gladness and for equanimity. Two things stand out.
First, the practice has an order. It doesn't start with everywhere. It starts with one direction and widens, the way sound travels out from one breath.
Second, measureless is the whole point.
That's why these four are called the immeasurables. A kindness that stops at the edge of my people, or my street, has a measure.
This one keeps going, the way the conch keeps sounding past the last house, until there's no edge left to stop at.

how: In Buddhist communities this practice is called radiating or pervading the brahmaviharas: practitioners send kindness, compassion, gladness and equanimity outward direction by direction, often after first wishing well to themselves and to people near them.

o: a strict count of good deeds done each day
a list of rules for monks only
qualities of the heart with no limit or edge

games.q: match each piece of the Tevijja Sutta.
p: two young brahmins with a question

s: the practice begins by wishing well to everyone at once
it starts with one direction, then widens: second, third, fourth, above, below, everywhere.
the horn image comes from the Tevijja Sutta, DN 13
the Buddha uses it for a mind that reaches everywhere without strain.
the sweep is done only with kindness
the text repeats it for compassion, gladness and equanimity too.

games.q: two young brahmins ask the Buddha how to reach union with Brahma. how does he answer?
o: he refuses to use their words at all.
he describes a mind of kindness, compassion, gladness and equanimity filling every direction.
he tells them to study with a different teacher.
games.why: he answers in their own terms, and describes the four immeasurables spreading everywhere, like a horn heard in every direction.

practice: Send kindness one way first, in front of you: whoever is out there, may they be well.
Then to your right, behind you, to your left, above, below, and then everywhere at once, like the sound of the conch, with no effort to reach anyone.
If you have time, let compassion, gladness and equanimity follow, each one a little wave outward.

wordCard.voice: Appamaññā. The immeasurables, qualities with no measure or edge: like a horn blower heard in every direction without strain, a kind mind reaches everywhere, and nothing is left out.

orig.note: Pali appamaññā: the immeasurables, qualities with no measure or edge.

carryVoice: Your line: boundless. Like the conch, it doesn't pick who gets to hear it. See you tomorrow.
